tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Criminal History Record Information (15 M.R.S. ch. 310-A, §§ 2262-2264)

controllingAuthority.summary: Chapter 310-A permits a person to move, in the underlying criminal proceeding, to seal the criminal history record information relating to one specific eligible criminal conviction. Under § 2262 the conviction must be an eligible criminal conviction; at least four years must have passed since the person fully satisfied each of the sentencing alternatives imposed under 17-A M.R.S. § 1502(2); the person must not have been convicted of another crime in Maine and must not have had a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition since satisfying the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction; must not have been convicted of a crime in another jurisdiction in that period; and must have no presently pending criminal charges in Maine or elsewhere. Former § 2262(6), an age condition, was repealed by PL 2023, c. 666, § 3. 'Eligible criminal conviction' under § 2261(6)(A) means a current or former Class E crime other than one under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 11, and under § 2261(6)(B) five specifically listed marijuana offences committed before 30 January 2017. Relief is mandatory once proven: § 2264(5) directs that the court shall grant the motion where the person establishes each prerequisite by a preponderance of the evidence. A hearing is required and the Maine Rules of Evidence do not apply (§ 2264(4)). The current text reflects PL 2021, c. 674 as amended by PL 2023, cc. 409, 639 and 666 and PL 2025, c. 513, which became law without the Governor’s signature on 11 January 2026 and took effect on 29 July 2026.

exclusions: Every Class A, Class B and Class C crime. Chapter 310-A does not reach them.
Every Class D crime other than the five listed marijuana offences committed before 30 January 2017.
A current or former Class E crime under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 11 (sexual assaults), excluded by § 2261(6)(A).

A conviction of another crime in Maine, a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. former ch. 54-F or ch. 67 subch. 4, or a conviction in another jurisdiction, in each case since the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction (§ 2262(3) and (4)).
Any presently pending criminal charge in Maine or in another jurisdiction (§ 2262(5)).

A non-conviction disposition. § 2262 reaches a specific criminal conviction only, and filing this motion on a non-conviction is affirmatively wrong; those records are handled by operation of law under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2).
The exclusion set is the defining fact about Maine: the ordinary adult route reaches almost nothing, and the product's most valuable function here is to say no accurately and quickly.

waitingPeriods.duration: Four years from the date the person fully satisfied EACH of the sentencing alternatives imposed under 17-A M.R.S. § 1502(2) — imprisonment, probation, administrative release, licence suspension, fine payments, restitution and community service. The clock does not start at conviction and does not start at release, and an unpaid restitution or fine balance means it has not started at all.

geography.venue: The court in which the conviction was entered, in the underlying criminal proceeding (§ 2264(1)). CR-218 carries checkboxes for Superior Court, District Court and the Unified Criminal Docket. Where several motions are filed the court consolidates them to one location.

destination.name: Clerk of the court in which the conviction was entered
destination.detail: File the completed CR-218 with the clerk of the court of conviction. The clerk sets the matter for hearing under § 2264(1). Filing is in person or by mail; eFiling availability varies by county during the Maine eCourts rollout.

components.notes: Form CR-218, Motion to Seal Criminal History — the Judicial Branch's own form for this motion, published on the criminal forms list and named on the Judicial Branch sealing instructions. § 2263 requires only that the written motion briefly address each statutory prerequisite, and CR-218 does that in five numbered paragraphs mapping one to one onto § 2262. One conviction per motion; there is no continuation page. LegalEase completes the caption, court selection, docket number and the participant's own identifying and case facts. Paragraph 3 is NOT auto-answered — see the manual-completion item. Not retained by Master Library Edition 1.1, so the source relationship is authority-gated.

Participant instructions covering, in order: confirm the offence class at the time of conviction and the date every sentencing alternative was satisfied, including fines and restitution; file CR-218 with the clerk of the court of conviction; expect no fee but confirm with the clerk; the clerk sets a hearing and a hearing is mandatory with no consent or default path; the Maine Rules of Evidence do not apply and the movant carries a preponderance burden on each prerequisite, so bring the certified judgment and any proof of completion; the court issues a written order with findings and provides a copy to the participant and to the prosecutorial office; if granted and the conviction is one the State Bureau of Identification maintains, the court transmits notice electronically and the Bureau amends its records and mails notice of compliance. The instructions also carry the § 2264(7) lifetime rule in prominent terms, and state plainly what sealing does and does not reach.

tracks._participantInputsNote: What LegalEase asks. Paragraph 3 of CR-218 is deliberately not derived from these answers; see manualCompletionItems.

participantInputs.question: What is your full legal name as it appears on the court record, and any other name you were charged under?
What is your date of birth?
Which court entered the conviction — Superior Court, District Court, or the Unified Criminal Docket?
Which county and court location was that?
What is the docket number of the criminal case?
What crime were you convicted of, as it is named on the judgment?
On what date were you convicted?
What class of crime was it at the time you were convicted — Class E, Class D, or something else? Use the class shown on the judgment, not the class the offence carries today.
Was the offence a sexual assault offence under Title 17-A, chapter 11?
Was this a marijuana offence committed before 30 January 2017?
participantInputs.conditionDescription: Asked where the offence is a Class D crime, because the only Class D route is the five listed pre-2017 marijuana offences.

participantInputs.question: What did your sentence include — jail or prison, probation, administrative release, licence suspension, a fine, restitution, community service, or a combination?
On what date did you finish the LAST of those, including paying every fine and every dollar of restitution in full? If any balance is still owed, say so.
Since that date, have you been convicted of any other crime in Maine?

Since that date, has any criminal charge against you been dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition? People often describe this as 'it got dismissed', and it is a disqualifier here, so please answer carefully.
Since that date, have you been convicted of a crime in any other state, in a federal court, or in a tribal court?
Do you have any criminal charge pending right now, in Maine or anywhere else?
Do you have any Maine adult criminal conviction that is OLDER than the date you finished the sentence for this conviction?
Have you already asked a court to seal this conviction and been denied?

manualCompletionItems.item: Paragraph 3 of CR-218 — the assertion of no other adult criminal convictions in Maine
manualCompletionItems.whereInPacket: CR-218, numbered paragraph 3
manualCompletionItems.why: Paragraph 3 of CR-218 Rev. 7/24 reads in full: 'Defendant has no other adult criminal convictions in Maine and has not had a case dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition since completing their sentence for this offense.' The trailing time limit governs the deferred-disposition clause but not the convictions clause, so the form asks the participant to swear to an unbounded absence of Maine convictions while § 2262(3) bars only a conviction SINCE the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction. A participant with an old prior that predates the completion date is not disqualified by the statute but reads as disqualified on the form. LegalEase does not answer this paragraph either way: it prints it blank, sets out both readings in plain terms, and tells the participant to complete it themselves and to take advice before filing if they have an older prior.

rules.filing: File the completed and signed CR-218 with the clerk of the court in which the conviction was entered, in the underlying criminal proceeding (§ 2264(1)). One motion per conviction. Filing is in person or by mail; eFiling availability depends on where the county sits in the Maine eCourts rollout. Nothing else is required by statute or by the form.
rules.fees: No fee is expected. Administrative Order JB-05-26 (A. 3-26), effective 9 March 2026, lists no fee for a criminal post-judgment motion and provides 'Filing a Criminal Action, Traffic Infraction, or Civil Violation: No fee' in both Superior and District Court. The $60 post-judgment motion fee on that schedule is tied by its own terms to M.R. Civ. P. 55(b)(2), 59, 60(b), 62 and 66, which are civil rules, and does not reach a criminal post-judgment motion. Confirm with the clerk and do not promise a refund.
rules.feeWaiver: none expected, because no fee is expected. If a clerk does assess one, in-forma-pauperis status under M.R. Civ. P. 91 exempts a litigant from schedule fees during the pendency of the action, but that is a civil rule and its application to a criminal motion is unresolved. Do not route the participant to CV-067 or CV-191.
rules.notice: § 2264(3) directs notice to the prosecutorial office that represented the State in the underlying criminal proceeding; a different prosecutorial office may represent the State by agreement between the two offices. No written objection procedure and no fixed response period exists. The State appears at the hearing and is heard.
rules.service: No service obligation is imposed on the movant by the statute or by CR-218, and the form carries no certificate-of-service block. The packet tells the participant that notice is understood to be the court's, to confirm that with the clerk at filing, and to hand the clerk a courtesy copy for the prosecutorial office if asked. See the unresolved question on service.
rules.participantSignature: The defendant signs CR-218. There is an optional attorney line; having an attorney is not required. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank.

The participant wants to challenge the underlying conviction rather than seal it.
The State signals opposition.

unresolvedQuestions.question: Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. But 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) provides that the Criminal History Record Information Act does not apply to criminal history record information contained in the records of public judicial proceedings retained by the District Court, Superior Court or Supreme Judicial Court, and that public access to those records is as provided by rule or administrative order of the Supreme Judicial Court. § 2265 opens 'Notwithstanding Title 16, section 704' and does not mention section 708. Participant-facing copy must therefore say that sealing restricts what criminal justice agencies may disseminate and what appears on a State Bureau of Identification check, and must not say or imply that the court case disappears from a public docket search.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review approved Track 1 with limitations and nothing in current authority disturbs it. CR-218 is the Judicial Branch's own form for exactly this motion and § 2263 prescribes content rather than form, so official_pdf_fill is correct and a custom pleading would add risk with no benefit. The mechanism, venue, destination and components are settled. What is deliberately NOT automated is paragraph 3, where the form is broader than § 2262(3): the packet prints it blank and explains the difference rather than giving a false answer in either direction. The mandatory hearing is a packet instruction and a post-generation handoff, not a generation blocker. The § 2264(7) lifetime unsealing and self-reporting duty is built into the post-grant instructions because it is the sharpest edge in Maine and applies to this track alone.

limitations.statement: Maine seals; it does not expunge. The Judicial Branch says in terms that Maine does not have expungement and the record is not completely erased. Never use 'expungement' in Maine participant copy.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Criminal Conviction for Engaging in Prostitution (15 M.R.S. § 2262-A)
tracks.publicName: Sealing a conviction for engaging in prostitution

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 2262-A permits sealing of criminal history record information relating to a conviction for the former Class E crime of engaging in prostitution under 17-A M.R.S. former § 853-A, repealed in 2023. The person must not have been convicted of a violation of 17-A M.R.S. §§ 852, 853, 853-B or 855, or of substantially similar conduct in another jurisdiction, and one year must have passed since the person fully satisfied each sentencing alternative for the conviction. Section 2262 opens 'Except as provided in sections 2262-A and 2262-B', so the general track's clean-record conditions in § 2262(3) and (4) and its pending-charge restriction in § 2262(5) do NOT apply here. Relief is mandatory: the information must be sealed if the conditions are met, and § 2264(5) requires the court to grant on a preponderance showing. Enacted by PL 2023, c. 409, § 2 and amended by PL 2025, c. 513, §§ 8 and 9, effective 29 July 2026, which repealed the eligible-criminal-conviction prerequisite formerly in § 2262-A(1). PL 2025, c. 513 also amended § 2264(7) so that the lifetime unsealing and self-reporting rule does not apply to a record sealed under this section.

exclusions: Any prostitution-adjacent offence other than 17-A M.R.S. former § 853-A. This is a named-offence route and it does not stretch.

A person convicted of a violation of 17-A M.R.S. § 852 (aggravated sex trafficking), § 853 (sex trafficking), § 853-B (engaging a person in prostitution) or § 855 (patronizing prostitution of a minor or a person with a mental disability), or of substantially similar conduct in another jurisdiction. The disqualifier is not time-limited on the face of the statute.

The general track's restrictions do NOT apply and must not be imposed here: there is no clean-record condition under § 2262(3) or (4) and no pending-charge restriction under § 2262(5), because § 2262 excepts this section in terms.

destination.name: Clerk of the court in which the conviction was entered
destination.detail: File the completed CR-289 with the clerk of the court of conviction. The clerk sets the matter for hearing under § 2264(1).

components.notes: Form CR-289, Motion to Seal Criminal Conviction for Engaging in Prostitution — the Judicial Branch's dedicated form for this named-offence route, directed by the Judicial Branch instruction page. Its three numbered paragraphs track § 2262-A. Retained by Master Library Edition 1.1 at Rev. 10/24 as a source-gated acroform of one page and fourteen fields. Rev. 10/24 predates PL 2025, c. 513: paragraph 1 still recites eligibility 'under 15 M.R.S.A. § 2261(6) and § 2262-A', but c. 513 repealed the § 2262-A(1) eligible-criminal-conviction prerequisite, so the form asserts a requirement the statute no longer imposes. That recital is left as a manual completion item rather than affirmed on the participant's behalf.

Participant instructions covering: this is a named-offence route reaching 17-A M.R.S. former § 853-A only; the one-year clock runs from full satisfaction of every sentencing alternative; the general track's clean-record and pending-charge restrictions do NOT apply here and the participant should not be discouraged by them; a hearing is required and there is no consent path on this section; there is no self-reporting duty and a later conviction does not unseal a § 2262-A record, which is a real advantage over the general track and is surfaced; and the CR-289 paragraph 1 recital is out of date, what that means, and why it is left blank. The instructions also carry the survivor-route screen described below.

tracks.legalName: Confidential Criminal History Record Information for Non-Conviction Dispositions, and the § 709 Inspection and Correction Request (16 M.R.S. ch. 7)
tracks.publicName: Cases that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Maine does not seal or expunge non-convictions on motion. Under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2) the listed non-conviction dispositions are confidential criminal history record information BY OPERATION OF LAW, with no filing and no court involvement: a summons or arrest without disposition where more than one year has elapsed, no active prosecution is pending and the person is not a fugitive; a decision by law enforcement not to refer to a prosecutor; a decision by a prosecutor not to initiate or approve criminal proceedings; a grand jury finding of insufficient evidence; a charge dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement; an acquittal, which does not include a verdict or accepted plea of not criminally responsible by reason of insanity; a mistrial with prejudice; termination for lack of subject matter jurisdiction; termination for want of jurisdiction over the defendant; and the remaining paragraphs of § 703(2), which include a pardoned conviction. Confidential information may be disseminated only to the recipients listed in § 705, and a criminal justice agency may not confirm its existence or nonexistence to anyone not entitled to receive it. Separately, § 709 gives a person the right to inspect their own criminal history record information held by a Maine criminal justice agency and to request that it be amended or corrected: the agency has fifteen days to investigate and notify the requester with reasons for any refusal, the agency head must complete an administrative appeal within thirty days, a person denied on appeal may file a statement of disagreement that must accompany any future dissemination, final agency action is appealable to the Superior Court under 5 M.R.S. ch. 375 subch. 7, and on correction the agency must notify prior recipients within thirty days. Section 709(6) provides that the section does not apply to court records, access to which is governed by Supreme Judicial Court rules.

exclusions: A dismissal that WAS part of a plea agreement. § 703(2)(G) reaches a dismissal with finality by a prosecutor OUTSIDE a plea agreement, and this is the most commonly misunderstood point in Maine.

A dismissal without prejudice does not become confidential merely because it was a dismissal. It reaches confidentiality only through the summons-or-arrest-without-disposition category, and only where more than one year has elapsed, no active prosecution is pending and the person is not a fugitive.
A verdict or accepted plea of not criminally responsible by reason of insanity, which § 703(2) does not treat as an acquittal.

Court records. § 709(6) says the section does not apply to them and 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) puts records of public judicial proceedings outside the Criminal History Record Information Act entirely, with public access governed by Supreme Judicial Court rule or administrative order. A publicly accessible docket entry is not cured by § 703(2) confidentiality.
Records held by a private background-check vendor, which chapter 7 does not bind. That is the business screening service track.
A charge dismissed after a completed deferred disposition, whose status under § 703(2) is not established. It routes through the deferred-disposition node and the packet promises nothing.

units.label: Confidentiality by operation of law — classification and verification, no filing
units.description: The base branch. Where the disposition falls inside the 16 M.R.S. § 703(2) list the record is already confidential criminal history record information and there is nothing to file: no court has any role, no motion exists, and generating CR-218 for a non-conviction would be affirmatively wrong because § 2262 reaches a specific criminal conviction only. The unit classifies the disposition against the § 703(2) list, explains that the confidentiality is automatic, walks the participant through obtaining their own State Bureau of Identification record to see what the State actually holds, and states plainly where the disposition falls outside the list that Maine offers no relief for it rather than routing them to a motion that will be denied. It also separates the three problems that participants conflate: the Bureau record, the court docket, and a private vendor's database.

units.label: 16 M.R.S. § 709 inspection and correction request to the criminal justice agency
units.description: The conditional branch, reached only where the agency record is demonstrably inaccurate — most often where the State Bureau of Identification is still carrying a disposition that § 703(2) makes confidential, or is carrying a disposition that is simply wrong. § 709(1) and (2) give the participant the right to inspect their own criminal history record information and to request that it be amended or corrected by contacting the agency, and the agency then has fifteen days to investigate and notify the requester with reasons for any refusal. No official Maine form exists for the request and none is prescribed by the statute, so this is a participant-signed written request that LegalEase drafts: it identifies the participant and the record, states the disposition and its § 703(2) category, states precisely what the agency record says and what it should say, attaches the disposition order, and asks for amendment or correction under § 709(2). The packet also carries the escalation path — administrative appeal to the agency head within thirty days, the statement of disagreement that must accompany any future dissemination, and Superior Court review of final agency action under 5 M.R.S. ch. 375 subch. 7 — as instructions rather than as generated documents. This unit is a separate legal act from unit 1: it has a participant submission, a named destination, its own statutory basis and its own legal output, where unit 1 has none of those.

unresolvedQuestions.question: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2). This was checked against current official text and is NOT ESTABLISHED. Section 703(2) lists paragraphs A through L and none mentions a deferred disposition. The closest is paragraph G, which reaches a charge 'dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement'. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 the State dismisses the charging instrument WITH PREJUDICE on compliance, which fits the first clause, but a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State, which arguably falls inside paragraph G's outside-a-plea-agreement carve-out. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. No statute, State Bureau of Identification guidance, Judicial Branch page or Law Court decision resolves it. The packet therefore fails closed: it does not promise confidentiality on the strength of the deferred-disposition label, it tells the participant to verify what the Bureau record actually shows, and it routes the correction request only where the record is demonstrably inaccurate.

controllingAuthority.summary: A deferred disposition is not a record-clearing mechanism and produces no relief of its own. It is a disposition status with two possible outcomes and one sharp cross-track consequence, and it is modelled as a routing node for exactly that reason. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1901 a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State; under § 1903, on compliance and the State's motion, the court permits withdrawal of the plea and the State dismisses the charging instrument with prejudice. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. Where the case instead ends in conviction of a reduced offence, that conviction is evaluated on its own terms under chapter 310-A and qualifies only if it lands inside the § 2261(6) eligible set. The cross-track consequence is the one that matters most: under 15 M.R.S. § 2262(3) a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition, since the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction, is an absolute disqualifier for the general sealing track. A deferred disposition is therefore good news for the case it resolves and bad news for a prior conviction the participant wanted sealed.

tracks.legalName: Business Screening Service Dispute for Correction or Deletion of Criminal History Record Information (10 M.R.S. c. 239, § 1500-CC)
tracks.publicName: Getting a sealed record off a background check

controllingAuthority.summary: Chapter 239 regulates how a business screening service handles Maine criminal history record information. A business screening service under § 1500-AA is a person regularly engaged in the business of collecting, assembling, evaluating or disseminating criminal history record information about specific individuals for a fee, excluding a government entity and the news media. Under § 1500-CC, where the completeness or accuracy of a record is disputed by its subject, the service shall investigate WITHOUT CHARGE; must review and consider all relevant information the subject submits and determine whether its record accurately reflects the official record maintained by the State Bureau of Identification; must correct a record that does not accurately reflect the official record; and — the operative remedy here — if the disputed record is found to be sealed or the subject of a pardon, SHALL PROMPTLY DELETE the record. The service may terminate an investigation it reasonably determines is frivolous, but must then state the specific reasons and describe the information it needs. Within thirty days of receiving notice of the dispute the service must notify the subject of the results, including whether the investigation was completed or terminated and what records were corrected or deleted. Section 1500-DD requires a service disseminating records collected on or after 1 July 2010 to include the collection date and a notice that the information may include records that have been sealed or otherwise become inaccessible since. Section 1500-EE provides an FCRA safe harbour, deems foreign-corporation screening services to consent to Maine jurisdiction, and supplies a private right of action. Enacted by PL 2025, c. 513, § 1 and effective 29 July 2026.

components.notes: The participant-signed business screening service dispute letter. No official form exists, no statute prescribes one, and none could: the duty runs against a private company rather than an agency. LegalEase drafts a controlled letter carrying the vendor's identity and dispute address; the report in which the record appeared and its date; the record exactly as the vendor reported it; the correct status, namely that the record is sealed by court order or is the subject of a pardon; a citation to § 1500-CC(2) and its prompt-deletion duty where the record is sealed or pardoned; a citation to § 1500-CC(4) and the thirty-day notification duty; a list of what is enclosed; and a signature block for the participant. This is correspondence to a private company, not a court pleading, and the packet says so in terms. The letter does not demand the § 1500-EE(3) statutory penalty, actual damages, costs or attorney's fees, does not threaten litigation, and does not assert an FCRA claim.

The supporting checklist and enclosure list: a copy of the court's written sealing order or the pardon, which § 1500-CC(2) makes the operative document for the deletion remedy; and, where the vendor's record differs from the official record on facts other than sealing status, a copy of the participant's own State Bureau of Identification record, which § 1500-CC(1) makes the comparison benchmark. The checklist names each item and tells the participant to enclose copies rather than originals. LegalEase does not inspect, authenticate or take custody of either document.

Instructions covering: how to identify the vendor and confirm it meets the § 1500-AA definition; how to send the letter so receipt can be evidenced, because the thirty-day clock runs from receipt; the calculated thirty-day follow-up date; what the three possible outcomes look like — correction, deletion, or a frivolousness determination that must state specific reasons and describe the information the service needs; that the investigation must be conducted without charge; the § 1500-DD collection-date and sealed-record notice that a compliant service must carry; and a plain statement that this route binds screening services only and reaches neither the Bureau record nor the court record. The instructions also state where self-help ends.

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 2262-B provides that criminal history record information relating to an eligible criminal conviction as described in § 2261(6)(C) must be sealed if the person filing the motion establishes, first, that the person has been a victim of sex trafficking or sexual exploitation, and second, that the commission of the crime for which the person was convicted was a substantial result of that sex trafficking or sexual exploitation. A motion under the section may be filed AT ANY TIME after the criminal conviction is entered. Section 2261(6)(C) defines an eligible criminal conviction for a § 2262-B motion as a criminal conviction for ANY current or former crime: there is no class limit, no chapter 11 exclusion and no offence list. Section 2261(8) defines sex trafficking and § 2261(9) defines sexual exploitation as engaging in the exchange of sex for money or resources because of a person's history of trauma, adverse childhood experiences, substance use disorder or other circumstances of victimization, exploitation or oppression. Section 2264(4-A) provides for remote participation by the person and any witnesses unless the court finds the person or a witness resides in Maine and the interests of justice require in-person participation; provides that official documentation of victim status is NOT required, and that if presented it creates a presumption that the person's participation in the offence was a substantial result of the trafficking or exploitation; and enumerates qualifying documentation, including an official record, certification or eligibility letter from a federal, state, tribal or local proceeding including a federal immigration approval notice, an affidavit or sworn testimony from clergy, a medical professional, victim services staff or another professional, and any other evidence the court finds of sufficient credibility or probative value. Section 2264(5) requires a hearing on a motion under the chapter EXCEPT that for a motion under § 2262-B the court may grant the motion without a hearing if the representative for the State consents. Section 2264(7), as amended, does not apply to records sealed under § 2262-A or § 2262-B, so a later conviction does not unseal and there is no self-reporting duty. Enacted by PL 2025, c. 513 and effective 29 July 2026.

exclusions: None on the face of the statute as to offence. § 2261(6)(C) reaches a conviction for any current or former crime, with no class limit, no Title 17-A chapter 11 exclusion and no offence list. This is by a wide margin the broadest sealing route in Maine.

No waiting period, no sentence-completion requirement, no pending-charge restriction and no case-count limit apply. The motion may be filed at any time after the conviction is entered, including while the person is still serving the sentence.

What the route does exclude is a case in which the two statutory elements cannot be established. That is a merits question for the participant and their advocate, not an eligibility filter LegalEase applies.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The retained review's single largest Maine build blocker — that CR-307 was unverified and might not exist — is closed. Master Library Edition 1.1 retains CR-307 at Rev. 06/26 as a source-gated acroform, and the current Judicial Branch forms list confirms it effective 29 July 2026 alongside a companion order form, CR-308, which the review recorded as not applicable. The track is therefore official_pdf_fill on a verified current form set and is modelled as ONE participant-facing court packet: screening, advocate assessment, filing and hearing happen at different times but are not legally distinct submissions, so the route is not composed. Packet identity and direct delivery scope are kept separate, exactly as the adopted memorandum requires for specialized routes. What LegalEase generates is the neutral case fields on CR-307 and the caption on CR-308. What it never generates is the survivor's account, the causal argument, or any determination that the participant meets the statutory victim status or the substantial-result test — and it asks one gentle screening question with no follow-up. A mandatory attorney, legal-aid or qualified-advocate assessment precedes preparation, and no document upload, staff approval, proof-of-review field or generation gate is introduced, because the product schema requires none.
